To form the passive in all tenses: être (in the required tense) + agreeing participle.
To introduce the agent with "par" (action) or "de" (state, feeling).
To use the pronominal passive: ça se vend, ça se dit, ça se fait.
To replace the passive with "on" in speech: on a créé une bourse.
To understand the language of the press and television.
Monday, 1 July 2029. A regional TV crew is filming at the Conservatoire. The journalist interviews Claire Vasseur about the new "Henri et Hélène" grant.
Madame Vasseur, thank you for having us. Can you explain how this grant was created?
It was bequeathed to the Conservatoire by an eighty-seven-year-old lady, Hélène Morel, who passed away in May. All her savings were given to the children of La Duchère.
Henri was the man she had loved at twenty. A waltz had been written by him in 1962. It was found again sixty years later, in an old piano.
It’s an incredible story. And how are the winners chosen?
They will be chosen every year by a jury of three people. The first jury was formed yesterday: myself, Julien Moreau and Madame Odile Bernard.
Odile Bernard… Henri’s widow, isn’t she?
Exactly. Hélène was keen for her to be on the jury. It was written in her letter. Those two women were very close, you know.
Have the first winners already been chosen?
Yes. The decision was taken this morning, unanimously. But the names won’t be announced until Friday, during the end-of-year concert.
(smiles) No. It isn’t done. The children must hear it first. But I can tell you that we found it very hard to choose.
This report will be broadcast tonight on the evening news. A final word?
Hélène was loved by everyone who knew her. Thanks to her, children who would never have been noticed will be able to become musicians. It’s the finest of legacies.
had ("avait aimé" = had loved; "avait été écrite" = had been written)
was keen ("tenir à ce que" = to be keen that)
difficulty ("avoir du mal à" = to find it hard to)
"A ay-tay kray-ay": three e’s in a row in "créée", pronounced as one long "ay".
Passive = ÊTRE in the required tense + past participle, AGREEING with the subject. The tense of the passive is given by the verb "être":
Don’t forget the agreement! "La bourse a été créÉE" (feminine), "les noms seront annoncÉS" (masculine plural). "Été" never changes.
The agent (the one doing the action) is usually introduced with PAR. But with verbs of FEELING or STATE, DE is used:
La valse a été écrite par Henri.
Les lauréats seront choisis par un jury.
Il est respecté de ses élèves.
La bourse a été léguée par Hélène.
Verbs with "de": aimer, détester, respecter, admirer, connaître, entourer, couvrir, accompagner (sometimes). When in doubt, "par" is safer.
French often uses a REFLEXIVE verb with a passive meaning, for general truths, habits or rules (like Romanian "se vinde", "se spune"):
Romanian does exactly the same, so it’s a natural structure for you. Just note: it has no agent ("se vend par…" is wrong).
In everyday speech, the French avoid the passive and use "ON" (someone, people, we):
La décision a été prise ce matin.
On a pris la décision ce matin.
Le reportage sera diffusé ce soir.
On va diffuser le reportage ce soir.
Some verbs can’t be put into the passive in French, especially those with an indirect object: "On m’a dit" CANNOT become "J’ai été dit". You can only say "On m’a dit" (I was told).
The French press loves the passive and nominalisation (ch. 50): "Une bourse créée par une retraitée", "Annonce des lauréats vendredi".

The jury had met on Sunday 30 June, in Claire Vasseur’s office at the Conservatoire. It was very hot. The windows were open onto the Saône, and you could hear the boats going by. On the table, thirty-six files had been laid out, one for each child in the orchestra.

Each file had been prepared by Julien over several weeks. It contained a letter from the child, a letter from the parents, the teacher’s opinion and a recording of a few minutes, made during rehearsals. Julien had listened to each recording at least ten times. He knew them by heart.

Odile was sitting opposite him, with her glasses and a notebook. She had been appointed to the jury by Hélène herself, in her letter, and she took the role very seriously. "I’m not a musician," she had said when she arrived. "But I was a paediatrician for forty years. I know how to recognise a child who needs someone to believe in them."

The rules of the grant had been drawn up by the notary, following Hélène’s instructions. They were very simple: every year, one child from La Duchère would be chosen to continue their studies at the Conservatoire, with an instrument, free lessons and a little money for scores and travel.

One single child. That was the problem. They had spent four hours listening, reading, discussing. They had eliminated names, then put them back. By the end of the afternoon, two were left. And none of the three wanted to choose between them.

Inès, on one side. Eleven, shy, almost mute when she had arrived in September. Today she played Lucien Roux’s clarinet as if she had been born with it. Madame Roux said she played better than her husband, which, according to her, wasn’t difficult, but was still a very great compliment.

Yanis, on the other. Eleven too. The first to stand up, the last to leave. The boy who had played in front of a hundred and fifty councillors and tipped a vote. The son of a man who had given up music to work nights, and who was finding it again thanks to him.

"We can’t choose," said Odile, taking off her glasses. "If we take one, the other will be crushed. And Hélène wouldn’t have wanted that." Claire sighed. "The rules say one child a year. The money has been calculated for one. I don’t see how else we can do it."

There was a long silence. Then Odile opened her bag and took out an envelope. It was the one Hélène had left her on 3 May. Nobody knew what it contained. Odile had kept it sealed for two months. She put it on the table, in front of Claire.

"Hélène wrote me a personal letter," she explained. "In it she tells me things that concern only the two of us. But at the end there’s a sentence for the jury. She had foreseen this moment, I think." She unfolded the last page and read, in a slightly trembling voice:

"If one day the jury hesitates between two children, Odile, give it this cheque. It’s the money I had put aside for a trip to Seville that I never took. It will be better used this way. And tell them never to choose between two children when they can help two."

In the envelope was a cheque. It had been signed in April, during the nights of fever, in handwriting so shaky it was barely recognisable. The sum was exactly what was needed for a second grant for ten years. Claire sat for a long time without saying anything, the cheque in her hand.

Julien stood up and went to the window. He looked at the Saône so that no one would see his eyes. Outside, a boat was going slowly by, and someone on deck was whistling a song. It wasn’t the waltz. But Julien smiled anyway. "She had foreseen everything," he said softly. "Even this."

The decision was taken unanimously a few minutes later. Two winners: Inès and Yanis. The names would only be announced the following Friday, at the end-of-year concert, in front of the families. Until then, the secret had to be kept. Not even the parents would be told.

On Monday 1 July, a crew from regional television came to the Conservatoire. The story of the grant had been told in the local paper, and the television wanted to make a report on it. They interviewed Claire, then went to film a rehearsal in La Duchère.

The children were very excited by the cameras. They combed their hair, pushed to get into the front row, pulled faces behind the journalist’s back. Julien had a hard time getting them to play seriously. In the end it was Yanis who calmed them down, tapping his cello with his bow, like a conductor.

The report was broadcast that same evening, on the seven o’clock news. The whole family had gathered at Ioana and Julien’s to watch it: Odile, Radu, Lucia, and even Victor, settled on the sofa as if he had been invited. Ioana had made crêpes. Nobody ate them.

The report lasted three minutes. You saw the Conservatoire, then La Duchère, then the children playing. You saw Yanis, very serious, and Inès, eyes closed. And then, for a few seconds, you saw a photo: an old lady in a hat, in a wheelchair, her hand resting on a stone.

Odile put her hand over her mouth. Ioana took Julien’s hand. Rose-Hélène, sitting on her father’s lap, pointed at the screen and said, very clearly: "Néné." It was the name she had been calling Hélène for months. Nobody could answer. Victor began to purr.

The following days were the hardest for Julien. The secret had to be kept, but the children sensed something was coming. During rehearsals they looked at him with eyes full of questions. Inès played even better than usual, as if she had guessed. Yanis arrived an hour before everyone else.

On Wednesday, Madame Mansouri was waiting for him at the exit, arms folded. "Monsieur Moreau," she said, "people in the neighbourhood are saying a grant will be given on Friday. My son isn’t sleeping any more. He has to know." Julien smiled and gave the only answer he was allowed to give: "Come on Friday. And bring your husband."

On Friday 5 July, the end-of-year concert took place in the school’s covered playground, for the last time. After the summer, the orchestra would move into the new room, if the work was finished in time. The playground had been decorated by the children with garlands, drawings and a large photo of Hélène.

The concert was a success. The children played every piece they had learned during the year, from "Au clair de la lune" to "The Foundation Stone". The parents applauded every piece as if it had been played by the Opera orchestra. Madame Roux, in the front row, never stopped crying.

Then Claire Vasseur went up onto the little platform. She explained the story of the grant in a few simple sentences. She spoke of Hélène, of Henri, of the waltz. Then she said that at first only one winner was to be chosen. The children held their breath. So did the parents.

"But Hélène had foreseen everything," Claire went on. "Even our hesitations. Thanks to her, this year there won’t be one winner. There will be two." She opened an envelope. "The winners of the first Henri and Hélène grant are… Inès Benali and Yanis Mansouri."

There was a second of silence, then an explosion. The children shouted, jumped, banged on their buckets. Inès stood motionless, the clarinet in her arms, as if she hadn’t understood. Then she burst into tears. Madame Roux got up from her chair, which she hadn’t done without help for months, and went to take her in her arms.

Yanis didn’t shout. He turned towards the back of the hall, where his father was standing in his work uniform, straight from his night shift. Monsieur Mansouri said nothing. He just raised both arms above his head, like a fan when his team has scored a goal.

After the concert, a young journalist from the local paper asked Monsieur Mansouri how he felt. He thought for a moment, then said a sentence that was published on the front page the next day: "My son will be the first musician in the family to be paid to play. I was paid to keep quiet."

The concert ended with Henri’s waltz, played by the whole orchestra. And while the children were playing, Radu and Lucia slipped up to the platform, hand in hand. When the waltz was over, Radu took the microphone, a little red. He had an announcement to make, and he had asked Julien’s permission.

"Lucia and I are getting married," he said. "The date was chosen last night. It will be Saturday 4 May next year. The day after the 3rd of May. So that the waltz is played the day before, and we can dance the day after." The children applauded without understanding everything. Odile had understood. She was smiling.

Lucia took the microphone in turn. "And we have a request," she added. "We’d like the La Duchère orchestra to play at our wedding. All evening. With the buckets." There was a howl of joy. The youngest boy in the orchestra, the one who wanted a slide, asked if there would be ice cream. Lucia promised there would.

That evening, on the way home, Odile asked Julien to drop in at hers for a minute. She showed him Hélène’s letter, her own, the one she had kept for two months. She didn’t show him the first pages. Only the last one, with the sentence for the jury.

At the bottom of the page, under the signature, there was a postscript that nobody had seen, written even smaller than the rest. Julien had to hold the letter up to the lamp to read it: "PS: And if the jury chooses a child who plays the cello, tell them that Henri dreamed of playing it. He could never afford to."

Julien reread the sentence three times. Then he looked up at Odile. "Did you know?" Odile shook her head. "No. He never told me. In forty years he never told me." She smiled, her eyes shining. "There were still things I didn’t know about him. Hélène knew them."

The next day, Julien went to La Duchère. Yanis was there, in front of the site, watering the lime tree with his red watering can, as he did every morning. Julien sat down on the bench and read him the postscript. Yanis listened without moving. Then he put down the watering can.

"Then I’ll play for him too," he said, very seriously. "For Henri. He couldn’t, but I can." He sat down next to Julien, on the bench, under the little lime tree. They stayed there a long time, without speaking, watching the workers put up the walls of the new room.

That report was seen by thousands of people. The newspaper article was read all over the region. But the most important sentence of that week was heard by only one man, on a bench, one summer morning: that of an eleven-year-old boy who had decided to play for someone he had never known.
